docs.explain: IF handles two outcomes, and the moment a question has three the nested IFs start multiplying parentheses until nobody can read them. IFS takes tests and results in pairs and returns the result of the first test that is TRUE. That is why the order of the pairs is the whole logic. Put the loosest test first and nothing else can ever be reached. A final pair of TRUE and a fallback is how a range that might be empty still returns something instead of #N/A. Leaving it out is the most common error with the function. In this drill Ben's 78 is tested against 90, then 80, then 70, and lands on C. Cleo's 85 in the second screen is labelled Pass, because Merit needs 90. Every test is a comparison on a cell in the grid, so changing a score re-bands the row without touching the formula. IFS is not available in very old versions of Excel, where nested IFs are the only route, so it is worth being able to read both forms.
